Pelagius
puh-LAY-jee-uhs
proper noun
The Latinized name of the British-born monk and theologian of the late fourth and early fifth centuries, opponent of Augustine.

📖 Biblical Definition

Pelagius was a British-born monk and moral teacher of the late fourth and early fifth centuries who became the great opponent of Augustine and the father of the heresy that bears his name. Scandalized by what he saw as moral laxity, and reading Augustine’s prayer “give what thou commandest, and command what thou wilt” as an excuse for sin, Pelagius taught a doctrine of human ability that denied original sin and the necessity of grace. He held that Adam’s sin injured only Adam, not his posterity, so that every man is born innocent, with a free will fully able to choose good or evil; that men sin only by imitation, not by inherited corruption; that grace is helpful but not necessary, an aid to what the will can in principle do without it; and that men may, by their own free choice and effort, keep the law of God and merit salvation. Augustine answered him decisively from Scripture, and Pelagianism was condemned as heresy by the councils of the church. The dictionary names Pelagianism as the archetypal denial of the gospel of grace, the doctrine that man can save himself. Scripture teaches the opposite at every point: in Adam all die, all have sinned, the natural man is dead in trespasses, no man is justified by the deeds of the law, and salvation is by grace through faith, not of works, lest any man should boast. Pelagius is remembered as the perennial type of every scheme—ancient or modern—that flatters human ability and denies the sinner’s helpless need of sovereign grace.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The British monk and opponent of Augustine who denied original sin and the necessity of grace, teaching that man by free will can keep God’s law and merit salvation—condemned as heresy.

expand to see more

PELAGIUS, the British monk and theologian, opponent of Augustine.

Denied original sin, holding every man born innocent with a free and able will.

Taught that men sin by imitation, not inherited corruption.

Held grace to be helpful but not necessary; man may merit salvation by effort.

Condemned as a heretic by the councils of the church.

Eph 2:8 — "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:"

Eph 2:9 — "Not of works, lest any man should boast."

Jer 13:23 — "Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Pelagianism denies original sin and the necessity of grace, teaching that man can save himself by free will and effort.

expand to see more

The corruption is Pelagianism—the doctrine that man, unfallen in nature, can by his own free will keep God’s law and earn salvation, with grace a mere help rather than a necessity. Scripture denies it root and branch: by one man sin entered the world and death passed upon all, for that all have sinned; the natural man is dead in trespasses; the Ethiopian cannot change his skin nor the sinner do good who is accustomed to evil; and salvation is by grace through faith, the gift of God, not of works, lest any should boast. Pelagius makes man his own saviour and grace superfluous, overthrowing the gospel.

The dictionary names Pelagianism the archetypal denial of grace, condemned by the early church and refuted by Augustine, whose recovery of the biblical doctrine the Reformers gladly claimed. Its semi-Pelagian and Arminian descendants soften but do not cure the error, still granting fallen man a decisive ability and crediting salvation partly to the human will. The dictionary holds the doctrines of grace against them all: man is dead and helpless in sin, salvation is wholly of the Lord, regeneration precedes and produces faith, and the glory of the sinner’s rescue belongs to God alone. Pelagius stands as the perennial type of every flattering scheme of human ability and self-salvation.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

His name marks the archetypal heresy of self-salvation—the denial of original sin and the necessity of grace.

expand to see more

Pelagianism — the heresy of human ability and self-salvation that bears his name.

Denied peccatum originale, original sin inherited from Adam.

Held the will liberum and able, needing grace only as a help.

Opposed by Augustine, the great doctor of grace.

Semi-Pelagianism and Arminianism are its softer descendants.

Usage

"Pelagius is named as the father of the heresy of self-salvation."

"Pelagianism is answered by the doctrines of original sin and sovereign grace."

"It is cited as the type of every modern scheme that flatters human ability."
